newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa focuses on pollution in new shipping law.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa focuses on pollution in new shipping law.

text.p: The South African Transport Ministry on Thursday tabled a wide-ranging shipping amendment bill including measures to extend oil pollution provisions to cover other harmful substances.
"The changes are largely administrative, but there are significant amendments to our pollution control regime," said Carl Briesch, the ministry's deputy director for shipping.

He said the amendment, likely to be adopted by parliament in the first half of this year, would shift crucial aspects of pollution control and prevention from national standards to fit provisions of the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, known as Marpol.
The proposed Shipping General Amendment Bill also would give the government extended power to intervene in the event of pollution or threatened pollution by harmful substances other than oil.
"At the moment, we don't have any effective legislation to deal with any other type of spill than oil," said Briesch.
"There is no special measure to cater for nuclear or radioactive substances off our coastline, but these would be covered by the extended general provisions," he added.
The amendment could give South Africa limited power to intervene on the high seas to deal with or to prevent a grave and imminent threat to South Africa's coastline or interests.

The bill proposes to double the maximum fine for the illegal discharge of oil off South Africa's coast to 500,000 rand ($112,000) and Briesch said this ceiling would be reviewed if it proved ineffective.
The amendment does not extend the existing shipowner's liability, which currently concerns only oil spills, but this would be dealt with in separate proposals, he said.
The proposal includes clauses to express insurance values in International Monetary Fund Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) instead of the Poincare gold franc.
